I like to write stories in my free time. One day, I hope that I can work on games so I can tell these stories through them. I've been writing stories for about seven years now (currently, I'm twenty), and I can say with certainty that for a good several years, they all fucking sucked. They were piles of shit that were basically just reskinned versions of whatever my most recent obsession was. One Piece, Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts, etc.

There's one story in particular that began life as basically a ripoff of Zelda which I've been working on, retooling, reskinning, scrapping and reconceptualizing for about five years. It's gone through about three "phases" so far, each radically different from the last but still retaining the best elements of each. The second phase had less influence from Zelda and more from One Piece and Kingdom Hearts. That one was shit too, but significantly less so. The third, has influences from Xenoblade and less from the prior three. Aside from overall tone and some themes (friendship and adventure, but also obligation and growing from adversity), it's much more "influenced" by them and less "ripping chunks of flesh from the inspiration's corpse". I don't think this third is a masterpiece.

I think that in some ways, it's trash. I expect that there may be a fourth phase in this story on the horizon. I've dumped five years of my life into this story, watched it grow and rise from utter shit to something that might not be too bad if I released as is. Mediocre, but not bad.

I suggest that you keep going. You don't need to have a 5+ year epic in the making to become creative. You just have to keep creating and striving to get better. Copy the people who made you want to start on this artistic journey, and keep iterating on it until you're not copying any more. Until you have your own style that you can iterate on. I sincerely hope that one day, when you can be satisfied with your work, I might be able to see it.

It sounds like you're a new artist so here is what I recommend. First stop beating yourself up because you're not creating the latest and greatest. When you see art realize you're watching the highlight reel of that individual. You're not seeing the failed projects, the dead ends, the slightly imperfect, the what-could-have-been-if-I-didn't, etc. Every artist going to have a boatload of terrible, unusable, god awful ideas and they are necessary to the creative process because you need to waddle through them in order to find the good ideas laying underneath. So find some mundane task and let your mind wander, let it explore what it can dream up and as you discard more and more ideas eventually you'll find something that speaks to you.

Next, there is nothing wrong with taking inspiration from someone else. Art and life are basically one big echo chamber and its not important who started it, its important to experience it and let it change you so that you grow as a person and an artist. The only time I can think of it being a problem is when you're working professionally as "The cheaper version of Person X," once Person X is no longer in style you'd be boned. So let your inspirations out and over time they'll start to shift and eventually your style becomes its own.

Lastly keep doing art for yourself. So long as you're happy doing it the rest can bugger off.

The issue, though, is that the thrust is so tiny, that until it's tested in space, it won't be neither disproved or confirmed in a way that will end all speculations. That comes to the main problem - to reliably test it in space we'd need to move it reasonably far away from earth LEO (maybe GEO or L2) to avoid interference from debris and earth's magnetic field.
